title: Three Lancasters Monument, Kortrijk/Bissegem
location_name: Overzetweg bridge over the Leie, Bissegem, Kortrijk, West Flanders, Belgium
squadron_display_name: 101 Squadron RAF (W4967 SR-P), 467 Squadron RAAF (LM101 PO-J), 9 Squadron RAF (PD205 WS-H)
station: RAF Ludford Magna (101 Sqn) / RAF Waddington (467 Sqn) / RAF Bardney (9 Sqn)
cause_of_loss: W4967 — nightfighter (Fw Karl Beyer, 1./NJG 4); LM101 — cause not confirmed; PD205 — anti-aircraft fire (1./Flak-Regiment 53, not nightfighter)
memorial_name: Monument for the Crews of Three Lancasters, Kortrijk/Bissegem
memorial_details: Polished Himalaya granite monument in the form of the vertical tail fin of a Lancaster bomber. Designed by Etienne Vanackere. Unveiled 21 July 2009 (65th anniversary) on the bank of the Leie at Wevelgemsevoetweg, Bissegem. Relocated approximately 100 metres to the new Overzetweg bridge site in autumn 2022 as part of a local infrastructure project. The front face commemorates the crew of PD205; the reverse honours the crews of W4967 and LM101.
crew_summary: Twenty-two killed in total across three aircraft; one survivor (WO2 Noble of W4967, POW). The raid on Kortrijk railway yards on 20/21 July 1944 also killed approximately 250 Belgian civilians.
narrative:
On the night of 20/21 July 1944, Bomber Command sent 302 Lancasters and 15 Mosquitos against the railway yards at Kortrijk, a crucial supply route behind German lines in occupied Belgium. Approximately 250 Belgian civilians died in the city and suburbs — a catastrophe that overshadowed the military objective in local memory for decades.

Three of the Lancasters failed to return in the Kortrijk area. W4967 of 101 Squadron — an ABC (Airborne Cigar) electronic-countermeasures aircraft carrying a dedicated eighth crew member to operate jamming equipment — was shot down by Fw Karl Beyer of 1./NJG 4 and came down near the Karmelietenklooster in the city centre. LM101 of 467 Squadron RAAF crashed near Marke on the south-western outskirts; the cause of loss for LM101 has not been confirmed from the sources consulted. PD205 of 9 Squadron was brought down by anti-aircraft fire from 1./Flak-Regiment 53 (not a nightfighter, as sometimes stated) and came down closer to the Leie at Bissegem, where the monument now stands. Twenty-one men died across the three aircraft; one — WO2 Noble of W4967 — survived injured as a prisoner.

The granite tail-fin monument unveiled in 2009 was the product of local Belgian initiative, designed to give the three crews a single visible point of remembrance in the landscape where they fell. The attendance of John Elliott, brother of Sgt Thomas Elliott of PD205, at the 2009 dedication illustrated the direct family connection that such local memorials sustain.

crew.name: G.A. Noble
crew.fate_detail: W4967 SR-P, 101 Squadron. Survived injured as prisoner of war.

crew.name: Thomas Leo Roberts
crew.fate_detail: LM101 PO-J, 467 Squadron RAAF. Listed as possible seventh crew member; name not independently verified from a primary source — five crew confirmed, Roberts listed in research but not cross-checked.

crew.name: Thomas Woodman Elliott
crew.fate_detail: PD205 WS-H, 9 Squadron RAF. His brother John attended the 2009 dedication ceremony.

community_connection: Monument designed by local Belgian sculptor Etienne Vanackere. John Elliott, brother of Sgt Thomas Elliott of PD205 (9 Squadron), attended the 2009 dedication ceremony. Monument relocated 2022 as part of a local bridge infrastructure project. Hangar Flying heritage organisation documents the site.
